items.question: what does this mean?
items.script:
say It's a matrix equation: a matrix times a vector x gives the vector b.
say Think of a recipe: two ingredients mixed in set amounts give one final dish.
note 440 170 260 150 | A x = b | Matrix A times unknown vector x equals b
say Here the board shows [2, -1; 1, 2] times [x, y] equals [0, 3], which is the system of equations.
say Where it breaks: a real recipe has no unknowns, but here we solve for x and y.
title Matrix form of linear equations

items.question: explain this like a story
items.script:
say Think of it as a story about two friends solving a puzzle together.
say Once upon a time, Ada had two clues, and each clue mixed x and y in its own way.
note 580 170 190 170 | Column of unknowns | x and y are the answers we are hunting for
say Her first clue was 2x minus y, and the second was x plus 2y.
say The puzzle needed both clues to hit exact targets, 0 and 3.
note 680 180 90 150 | Target vector | The right side: 0 and 3
say Where the story breaks: real puzzles are often messier, and matrices just keep the bookkeeping tidy.
title Matrix form as a story

items.question: show me step by step how to solve this
items.script:
say Correction: I misread the board earlier. The answer is x = 1 and y = 2.
say The first row says 2x minus y equals 0, so y equals 2x.
note 430 175 250 55 | Row 1: 2x - y = 0 | So y = 2x
say Put 2x into the second row: minus x plus 4x equals 3, so 3x = 3, x = 1.
say Then y = 2. Check: 2 minus 2 is 0, and minus 1 plus 4 is 3.
title Solving 2x - y = 0, -x + 2y = 3

items.question: how would they test this, exam style?
items.script:
say Expect "solve this system" with a matrix form, and you find x and y.
say The clue words are "solve" and a matrix equal to a vector. That means elimination or substitution.
note 430 175 250 55 | Pattern: 2x2 system | Two equations, two unknowns: solve for x and y
say Trap: forgetting to check your answer. Plug x and y back into both rows to catch slips.
say Want a twin problem with x + y = 5 and x - y = 1?
choices Yes, give me one | Not now
title Exam pattern: solving 2x2 systems

items.question: what is a matrix?
items.script:
say A matrix is a neat grid of numbers, in rows and columns, that packs a system into one object.
say Picture a seating chart: each seat holds one number, and the rows and columns keep them in order.
note 415 175 255 130 | The matrix A | Rows and columns of numbers, held in brackets
say Once upon a time, the board's clues were scattered; the matrix packed them into one tidy grid.
say Where it breaks: a seating chart is just a picture, but a matrix also does work, like multiplying a vector.
title What is a matrix?

items.question: why do we write it as a matrix?
items.script:
say We write it as a matrix to pack the whole system into one short line: A x = b.
say Picture Ada with two messy clues on sticky notes, mixing x and y in different amounts.
say Then she stacks the number-amounts into one grid, the matrix A, and the unknowns become a single column x.
note 680 180 90 150 | Target vector b | The right side: the targets 0 and 3
say Where it breaks: the grid is only notation, it doesn't solve anything until we do the work.
title Why write a system as a matrix?

items.question: what does the x mean here?
items.script:
say The x is the unknown: the number we are hunting for in the puzzle.
say Picture a locked box with two hidden numbers, x and y, and our clues are the only way to open it.
say In the matrix, x is one entry of the unknown column, and it has to match both clues at once.
say Where it breaks: x isn't a fixed value yet, it's the answer, which is 1 once we solve.
title What x means here

items.question: what is a system of linear equations?
items.script:
say A system of linear equations is a set of straight-line rules that must all hold at once.
say Picture two friends sharing one cookie jar: each rule says how the jar balances, and both must be true together.
note 430 175 250 55 | Two equations together | 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3, solved together
say Where it breaks: the friends share a jar in real life, but here we just need the x and y that fit both rules.
title What is a system of linear equations?

items.question: can you visualize this?
items.script:
say Yes: each equation is a line on a graph, and the answer is where the two lines cross.
say Picture the first rule, 2x minus y equals 0, as one straight line through the origin.
note 430 175 250 55 | Two lines | Each row is one line on the x-y graph
say The second rule is another straight line. The point where they cross is x = 1, y = 2.
title Visualizing a 2x2 system

items.question: explain this diagram
items.script:
say This network reads a handwritten digit and guesses which number from 0 to 9 it is.
say Each of the 784 input circles holds one pixel's brightness, from a 28 by 28 image.
note 240 300 60 45 | 784 inputs | One neuron per pixel of the image
say The middle columns pass signals along, finding shapes, until the last column of 10 gives the guess.
note 690 200 50 260 | 10 outputs | One neuron per digit, 0 to 9
title How a digit-reading network is laid out

items.question: what are these circles?
items.script:
say Each circle is a neuron, and it holds one number, like a dimmer switch.
say The brighter a circle looks, the bigger its number. Input circles show pixel brightness.
note 335 90 35 470 | Neurons | Each circle holds one number, shown by brightness
say Lines between circles carry each number onward, scaled by a weight, to the next column.
title What the circles are

items.question: what do the lines between them mean?
items.script:
say Each line carries a number from one neuron to the next, and multiplies it by a weight.
say Picture a dimmer: a thick line passes more of the signal, a thin one passes less.
note 380 120 90 410 | Weighted lines | Each line multiplies its signal by a weight
say The network learns these weights from practice, so the right ones make the right digit light up.
title What the lines between neurons mean

items.question: how does a neural network learn?
items.script:
say A network learns by nudging its weights until its guesses match the right answers.
say Picture a row of voters: each one hears the row before, weighs it, and passes a vote on.
say After a wrong guess, the weights that helped the wrong answer get quieter, and the right ones get louder.
note 690 200 50 260 | Right answer | The output that should light up for the digit
say Where it breaks: real voters don't adjust themselves; the network does this with math over many examples.
title How a neural network learns

items.question: explain this like a story
items.script:
say Think of the picture as a story about a digit trying to be recognized.
say Once upon a time, a handwritten 2 arrives as 784 tiny pixel brightnesses, all lit up in the left column.
note 45 88 145 146 | The digit 2 | The handwritten image the network reads
say Each column passes its signals on, weighted, until the last column of ten answers: which digit is it?
say Where it breaks: the story is one pass forward, but the real network learned its weights earlier, in training.
title Digit recognition as a story

items.question: quiz me on neural networks

note 240 300 60 45 | 784 inputs | Find what each input neuron holds

items.question: what is the input layer?
items.script:
say The input layer is the leftmost column: one neuron for each pixel of the image.
say Look at the 2 on the left. Its pixels feed the first column, so bright pixels make bright circles.
note 335 90 35 470 | Input layer | 784 neurons, one per pixel
say The 784 comes from a 28 by 28 grid, so the first layer holds the raw picture.
title The input layer

items.question: what is gradient descent?
items.script:
say Gradient descent is how a network slowly lowers its error, one small step at a time.
say Picture walking down a hill in thick fog: you can't see the valley, but you feel which way is steepest.
say Each step goes the downhill way, the network's weights shift a little, and the error shrinks.
say Where it breaks: you might stop in a small dip, not the lowest valley, so the answer can be good but not best.
title Gradient descent as walking downhill in fog

items.question: what is the output here?
items.script:
say The output is the network's answer: ten neurons, one for each digit from 0 to 9.
say Look at the right-hand column. The neuron that lights up most is the network's guess.
note 690 200 50 260 | 10 outputs | One neuron per digit, brightest is the guess
say For this picture, the goal is the 2 neuron, though the network's real guess depends on its trained weights.
title The output layer

items.question: show me visually how information flows
items.script:
say Information flows left to right: pixels in, then the middle columns, then ten guesses out.
say Picture a relay race: each column hands its numbers to the next, scaled by the weights.
note 335 90 400 470 | Left to right | Each column feeds the next, ending at the 10 outputs
say Nothing flows backward in this picture; training is the separate step that goes back to adjust weights.
title How information flows through the network

note 750 548 36 36 | CC button | Click to show or hide captions

items.question: explain how video streaming works
items.script:
say Streaming sends a video in small pieces, and your player plays each piece while the next one arrives.
say Picture a conveyor belt of lunchboxes: the kitchen sends one box at a time, and you eat each as it arrives.
note 20 68 932 526 | The video player | Pieces arrive and play; the player keeps some ahead
say When your connection is slow, the player may shift to a lower quality so the belt keeps moving.
say Where it breaks: a lunchbox is fixed, but video pieces can change quality as your internet changes.
title How video streaming works

items.question: what is a variable in python?
items.script:
say In Python, a variable is a name that stores a value, like x = 5.
say Think of a name tag stuck on a box: the tag is the name, and the box holds the value.
say So x = 5 puts the tag "x" on the value 5, and you can use x later to get 5 back.
say Where it breaks: a tag moves to a new box when you reassign it, so x = 7 means x now points at 7.
title Python variables as name tags

items.question: explain recursion
items.script:
say Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it.
say Think of nesting dolls: you open one, find a smaller doll inside, and open that too.
say The smallest doll that won't open is the base case, the stop point that ends the chain.
say Where it breaks: the dolls already exist, but recursion builds each smaller call as it goes.
title Recursion as nesting dolls

items.question: what is an API?
items.script:
say An API is a set of rules that lets one program ask another program for something.
say Think of a restaurant: the menu lists what you can order, and the waiter carries your order to the kitchen.
say You, the waiter, and the kitchen each have a job: you ask, the waiter passes it on, and the kitchen makes it.
say Where it breaks: a waiter can guess what you meant, but an API needs the request in exactly the right format.
title What is an API?

items.question: what is compound interest?
items.script:
say Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest, not just on the original money.
say Think of a snowball rolling downhill: it picks up snow, and the bigger it gets, the more snow it picks up.
say The starting money is the first snowball, each year's interest is new snow, and the next year's interest counts that snow too.
say Where it breaks: a snowball doesn't stop at a cliff, but interest needs time, and a bank pays it only when the rules say so.
title What is compound interest?

items.question: how do I solve 2x + 3 = 11?
items.script:
say The answer is x = 4: undo the plus 3, then undo the times 2.
say Step 1: subtract 3 from both sides, so 2x = 8.
say Step 2: divide both sides by 2, so x = 4.
say Check: 2 times 4 is 8, plus 3 is 11, so it matches.
title Solving 2x + 3 = 11

items.question: what is the derivative of x squared?
items.script:
say The derivative of x squared is 2x, found with the power rule.
say Pattern: "derivative of x to a power" means bring the power down, then subtract one from it.
say So x squared becomes 2 times x to the first power, which is 2x.
say Trap: writing 2x squared, forgetting to lower the power. The power drops by one because the rate of change of x squared is slower than x squared itself.
say Want a twin problem: the derivative of x cubed?
choices Yes, give me one | Not now
title Power rule for derivatives
